texto:
News stories about Celebrity Traitors drew 1 million page views across Taboola's publisher network in the week after the programme's second series began on October 1, 2026, according to a press release Taboola distributed on October 13. That is less than half the 2.2 million page views the same network recorded for Strictly Come Dancing in its first live week, even though Taboola's release puts the Celebrity Traitors television audience at 8.9 million, against 4.8 million for Strictly.
In Short
Taboola, a company whose software sits on news websites, counted how many times people opened articles about the TV show Celebrity Traitors in its first week back, and the answer was 1 million. That matters to publishers and advertisers because it shows which TV shows send readers to news sites, and the numbers suggest a bigger TV audience does not automatically mean more reading. The release leaves out exact dates, the list of websites and where the TV ratings came from, so the figures describe one company's network rather than the whole web.
What Taboola counted
The headline number is simple: 1 million page views for Celebrity Traitors news in "the first week since its return to screens," according to Taboola. Series two of the celebrity version of the reality show aired on October 1, with Richard E Grant, Maya Jama and James Acaster cast as traitors. Readership peaked at 371,200 page views the following day, October 2, "across Taboola's network of publishers," according to the company.
By PPC Land's calculation, that single day accounts for roughly 37% of the weekly total. Interest was front-loaded: the morning after the premiere did more than a third of the week's work.
The release does not name the product behind the data. Earlier Taboola readership releases covered by PPC Land - on Tesco Clubcard articles gaining 335,000 page views before a voucher deadline and on UK energy crisis readership rising 3,350% - attributed their figures to Taboola Newsroom, an editorial analytics tool that aggregates page views across sites using Taboola's technology. Those sites have included The Independent, National World titles and HuffPost UK. This release says only "Taboola's network of publishers." It does not say whether the count is limited to the UK, though the programme, the cast and the comparisons are all British.
The cast in page views
The individual figures run on a different clock. Taboola reports celebrity numbers over 45 days, not over the first week, and the release does not give the start or end date of that window.
Richard E Grant drew the most interest among the traitors. Taboola links this to what it called his "unfortunate traitor admission just moments after being given the role." News stories about the actor reached 604,000 page views over 45 days, according to the company. Maya Jama reached 110,000 and James Acaster 72,000 over the same period.
Among the faithful, the release lists:
- Michael Sheen: 169,000 page views
- Bella Ramsey: 87,000
- James Blunt: 74,000
- Leigh-Anne Pinnock: 56,000
The largest individual figure belonged to the presenter. Claudia Winkleman - spelled "Winkelman" throughout the release - received 722,000 page views over 45 days, 100,000 of them on October 1, according to Taboola.
Those numbers need care. A 45-day window that closes around the release date would open in late August, more than a month before the premiere. So a share of Grant's 604,000 page views could come from cast announcements, his film work or any other news about him. Winkleman's total almost certainly includes coverage unrelated to Celebrity Traitors, given that she was in the news this autumn for leaving Strictly. The celebrity figures also cannot be added to the 1 million weekly total, since they cover different periods and an article naming several cast members could count toward several of them. The release does not say how such articles are treated.
Television against reading
The more interesting part of the release is a comparison it makes almost in passing. Winkleman's "former show" Strictly Come Dancing also returned this autumn, and news stories about it reached 2.2 million page views in one week, according to Taboola. That figure first appeared in Taboola's earlier release, which PPC Land covered as Strictly stories drawing 2.2 million page views in a week, four times Emmerdale. That release also recorded Winkleman and Tess Daly leaving the Strictly presenting team, with Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe taking over.
"Although readership numbers favour the dancing show, TV viewership figures are higher for Celebrity Traitors," the release states. According to Taboola, Celebrity Traitors "reached an average of 8.9 million viewers - an increase from the 6.1 million average recorded at episode one of series one - and peaking at 9.1 million." Strictly, by comparison, averaged 4.8 million and peaked at 5 million.
Set side by side, the gap is wide. By PPC Land's calculation:
Celebrity Traitors had about 85% more average viewers than Strictly, yet Strictly produced 2.2 times the page views. Per viewer, Strictly generated roughly four times as much reading on Taboola's network. The 8.9 million average is also about 46% above the 6.1 million recorded for the first episode of series one, according to the release.
Why might that be? Taboola's release does not try to explain the gap, and page views alone cannot. Several structural differences are visible, however. Strictly runs for months with weekly live shows, results, judges' scores and a presenter change that generated its own coverage. The Strictly week Taboola measured also followed a launch show on September 19, according to the earlier release, so the first live week was not the first week of news. A linear TV rating counts people in front of a screen; a page view counts one load of one article. The two units were never designed to sit in the same sentence, and the release offers no method for converting one into the other.
There is also a wrinkle in the Strictly numbers. PPC Land's earlier piece noted that Strictly's live opener averaged 4.8 million against 6.2 million for the previous year's opener. Taboola now uses that weaker Strictly figure as the benchmark that makes Celebrity Traitors look large on television.
What the viewing figures do not say
The release names no source for its television data. It does not say whether the 8.9 million figure is an overnight number, a consolidated figure including catch-up viewing, or a measure that adds streaming on BBC iPlayer. It also does not say which episode or episodes the 8.9 million average covers. The phrase "an increase from the 6.1 million average recorded at episode one of series one" implies an episode-one comparison, but the release does not state that 8.9 million is the series-two opener. Nor does it name the broadcaster; both programmes air on the BBC.
What the release leaves out
Several definitions are missing from the document:
- Dates: "first week" is not defined. A week starting on the October 1 premiere would run to October 7, but the release does not say so. The 45-day window has no stated start or end.
- Scope: the release does not list the publishers in Taboola's network, the number of UK sites contributing, or whether non-UK sites are included.
- Article classification: it does not explain how a story is tagged as being about Celebrity Traitors or a specific cast member, or whether an article mentioning both Strictly and Celebrity Traitors counts for both.
- Engagement: page views do not show whether an article was read to the end, how long readers stayed, or whether the coverage was favourable.
- Previous series: no readership figure for series one is published, so there is no year-on-year readership comparison to match the year-on-year viewing comparison.
None of this makes the numbers wrong. It does mean the 1 million figure describes reading on sites that run Taboola's code, measured over a period the company chose, rather than total interest in the programme across the web.
The spokesperson's case
Dave Struzzi, Communications Lead at Taboola, framed the data around news supply rather than audience size. "Following the success of series one of Celebrity Traitors, it's no surprise readership is high this time around," he said, according to the release.
"The format of the show - like that of Strictly Come Dancing - with its various twists, turns and celebrity expulsions, ensure there is a constant stream of news angles from which publishers can capitalise," Struzzi said.
That second remark is the commercial point. Taboola's business depends on article pages that carry its recommendation units and ads. A programme that produces a new story after every episode creates more such pages, and more pages create more inventory for advertisers buying contextual advertising around entertainment news.
Why a recommendation company publishes TV readership
Taboola has issued a steady run of UK readership releases this year: the Ferrari Luce debut driving 1.04 million reads in a week across the US, UK and Italy in June, NBA Finals content outpacing the World Cup on game days the same month, the Clubcard data in August and Strictly at the start of October. Each shows publishers, and the advertisers who buy on those publishers, what Taboola's network can see.
The releases arrive at a delicate time for the company. When Taboola reported second-quarter results on August 5, revenue of $476.8 million came in $15.2 million below the bottom of its guidance range, and Google's back button policy ended a product Taboola had expected to add more than $20 million in ex-TAC gross profit in the second half of 2026, as PPC Land reported in Google policy cuts $20 million from Taboola's second-half profit. The company has been moving beyond its native recommendation widgets into open-web display through its Realize platform, and on August 19 gained NBC News display ads in its first deal beyond native. Taboola says Realize reaches approximately 600 million daily active users, a figure repeated in the boilerplate of this release.
It has also been courting publishers with on-site tools as search referrals fall. HuffPost UK adopted Taboola's DeeperDive answer engine in April, and in September Taboola extended its Goal.com deal to December 2028. Readership releases tied to big British TV moments serve that publisher-facing pitch: they suggest the network is where readers go when a programme becomes a talking point.
For advertisers, the useful signal in this release is narrower than the headline. Reading around a TV programme is concentrated in the first day after broadcast - 37% of the Celebrity Traitors week landed on October 2 - and it does not track audience size in any simple way. A show with nearly twice the viewers produced less than half the reading. Whether that reflects the programmes, the publishers in Taboola's network or the way articles are classified is something the release does not allow anyone to determine.
The release closes with Taboola's standard forward-looking statements disclaimer, which refers readers to the risk factors in the company's Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025.

Summary
Who: Taboola, the content recommendation and advertising company, with a quote from its Communications Lead Dave Struzzi. The figures concern the BBC programmes Celebrity Traitors and Strictly Come Dancing and cast members including Richard E Grant, Maya Jama, James Acaster, Michael Sheen and presenter Claudia Winkleman.
What: Taboola reported 1 million page views for Celebrity Traitors news in the first week of series two, with a peak of 371,200 on October 2, against 2.2 million in a week for Strictly. It also gave 45-day page view totals for individual celebrities and TV audience figures of 8.9 million on average for Celebrity Traitors and 4.8 million for Strictly, without naming the ratings source.
When: Series two premiered on October 1, 2026. Taboola distributed the release on October 13, 2026.
Where: Across Taboola's network of publishers, which the release does not list; the programmes and comparisons are British.
Why: The data shows publishers and advertisers how TV moments translate into article traffic on Taboola-powered sites. It also shows that a larger TV audience did not produce more reading: Strictly generated roughly four times as many page views per average viewer, by PPC Land's calculation.
